Designing a high-throughput, resilient file upload and download service in Java requires going far beyond simple MultipartFile handling. When scaling to handle gigabyte-sized payloads concurrently, you must solve memory exhaustion (OutOfMemoryError), thread starvation, and I/O bottlenecks. In a production-grade architecture, standard synchronous request-response models fail because they block valuable platform threads on slow socket reads and writes. Instead, modern upload/download engines leverage asynchronous I/O (NIO), non-blocking reactive streams, and direct off-heap memory transfers to stream binary data directly from the network socket to persistent storage without intermediate buffering in the JVM heap.

For uploads, the service must handle multi-part stream parsing safely, employing chunked transfers to write data incrementally to disk or object storage (such as Amazon S3) via asynchronous multipart upload APIs. For downloads, zero-copy mechanics using FileChannel.transferTo() allow the operating system kernel to pipe bytes straight from the disk cache to the network socket buffer, bypassing user-space memory entirely and slashing CPU utilization. Furthermore, robust architectures incorporate distributed rate limiting, cryptographic payload hashing (SHA-256) for integrity verification, and byte-range request processing to enable resumable downloads and parallel chunked transfers.

Supports HTTP Range headers for chunked resumes and parallel fetches

items: Zero-Copy Mechanics: Utilizing FileChannel.transferTo() lets the OS kernel transfer bytes from disk to network interface controllers (NICs) without CPU context switches between user space and kernel space.

Backpressure Management: In reactive implementations (e.g., Spring WebFlux with Project Reactor), data consumption speed is explicitly signaled by the consumer to prevent fast producers from overwhelming slow network clients.
Multipart Stream Parsing: Processing incoming multipart boundaries incrementally via reactive Flux<DataBuffer> streams prevents massive disk I/O amplification and garbage collection pressure.

parsed_answer.content: A classic 7+ YOE production trap in Java file transfers is attempting to read streams into byte arrays or using standard InputStream/OutputStream loops inside blocking thread pools under heavy load. This instantly causes thread pool starvation and triggers frequent Full GCs due to massive byte[] allocations in the Old Generation. Always offload blocking file I/O to a dedicated bounded elastic scheduler or leverage AsynchronousFileChannel, and enforce strict streaming limits to prevent malicious clients from sending unbounded payloads.
